extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / early-18th-century educated English public; writers and commentators
extracted.subtask_description: Producing short moral and social essays in the style of The Spectator (early 18th-century English periodical), emphasizing concise prose, moral effect, and domestic/social observation. Includes guidance on language, style, and the ethical/practical aims of such essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Est brevitate opus, ut currat Sententia ... (Hor.). The English tongue (and English writing) is adapted to be sparing of words and an enemy to loquacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver thoughts in the fewest words possible; pack matter closely so ideas lie in a narrower compass. Favor concision as a central design of speech and writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of monosyllables for clarity and speed
rubrics_metrics.description: The English abounds in monosyllables, which gives us an Opportunity of delivering our Thoughts in few Sounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer short, monosyllabic words where they convey the idea; this may lessen elegance but improves readiness and directness of expression (compared to more tunable multi-syllabic words).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contraction of multisyllabic (Latin-derived) words for dispatch
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the Words are not Monosyllables, we often make them so, as much as lies in our Power, by our Rapidity of Pronounciation; ... in many of our long Words which are derived from the Latin, where we contract the length of the Syllables ... to make them more proper for Dispatch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In rapid or familiar speech and writing, pronounce/shape longer words more compactly to suit the brisk English style; be mindful this affects tone (makes it less solemn) and register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviation of past-tense endings (-ed, -eth) in common usage
rubrics_metrics.description: The Abbreviation of several Words that are terminated in ed, by closing in one Syllable the Termination of our Præterperfect Tense, as in the Words, drown'd, walk'd, arriv'd; and the Abbreviation of several Words terminated in eth by substituting an s ... as in drowns, walks, arrives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that spoken and familiar written English commonly shortens these endings; note the effect on sound (more consonant clusters) and on perceived style or 'disfigurement' of the tongue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pruning spelling to match pronunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some celebrated Authors ... began to prune their Words of all superfluous Letters, as they termed them, in order to adjust the Spelling to the Pronunciation; which would have confounded all our Etymologies, and have quite destroyed our Tongue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not recklessly respell words to mirror colloquial pronunciation; preserve etymological spelling where important to maintain the language's structure and history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive clipping and colloquial contractions
rubrics_metrics.description: We have drawn two Words into one, which has likewise very much untuned our Language, and clogged it with Consonants, as mayn't, can't, shd'n't, wo'n't, &c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit the use of clipped forms and heavy contractions in writing that aspires to elegance; they may be acceptable in familiar contexts but can 'untune' the language if overused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve necessary particles and relatives for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: There is another Particular in our Language which is a great Instance of our Frugality of Words, and that is the suppressing of several Particles which must be produced in other Tongues to make a Sentence intelligible. This often perplexes the best Writers ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not omit essential particles (whom, which, that, etc.) when their presence is required for clarity; economizing words should not render sentences ambiguous or ungrammatical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and style should reflect national genius and temperament
rubrics_metrics.description: I have only considered our Language as it shows the Genius and natural Temper of the English, which is modest, thoughtful and sincere, and which perhaps may recommend the People, though it has spoiled the Tongue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let style serve the character of the audience/nation: English prose may favor modesty, thoughtfulness, and sincere brevity. Adapting tone to national or cultural temper can make writing more effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of subjects and capacity to both divert and improve
rubrics_metrics.description: The Variety of your Subjects surprizes me ... you charm the Fancy, sooth the Passions, and insensibly lead the Reader to that Sweetness of Temper ... you rouse Generosity with that Spirit, and inculcate Humanity with that Ease ... offer an infallible Cure of Vice and Folly, for the Price of One Penny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periodical essays should vary their topics, combine entertainment and instruction, engage readers emotionally (charm, soothe), and promote moral improvement with a light, accessible touch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not over-elaborate clear matters; avoid excessive circumstantiality
rubrics_metrics.description: One meets now and then with Persons who are extreamly learned and knotty in Expounding clear Cases ... It is pleasant enough to see such Persons contend without Opponents, and triumph without Victory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining simple or uncontested points, avoid unnecessary learning, minute particulars, or prolix proofs that burden the reader; be concise and stick to what advances the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Household leadership: equanimity, empathy, and temper in masters
rubrics_metrics.description: He who is not Master of himself and his own Passions, cannot be a proper Master of another. Æquanimity in a Man's own Words and Actions, will easily diffuse it self through his whole Family.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In essays offering social or moral advice, recommend that those in authority practice self-control, fairness, and empathy; such temper produces better domestic and social outcomes and is a standard by which masters may be judged.
